title: How do you handle comments from AI haters on Itch?
author: Daniele-Fantastico
selftext:
As expected, some comments from AI haters showed up on my game’s Itch page.

I’ve been developing games professionally for 15 years. So even though I used Claude Code, I can confidently say the game is good and definitely ready for release. It’s not sloppy or rushed work.

At first I felt like replying, but I held back.

Comments can be deleted or reported.  
In your experience, what’s the best strategy?  
Ignore them? Delete them?

Has anyone here been through this already?

replies.author: Daniele-Fantastico
replies.body:
So there are AI haters here too?

With my team, a few years ago we also created an artistic game, which is now exhibited at the MAXXI (Museo nazionale delle arti del XXI secolo) museum in Rome. In addition to having developed and published dozens of games on every platform. I started with C++, then moved on to various engines. Each time it became easier. The more modern engines practically allow anyone to publish games, most of the time extremely poor ones. Too often weak developers call themselves artists. I know developers who are truly artists, and they are few. For at least 10 years I have seen terrible games being released. Now AI is just another tool and you have to know how to use it. I mainly develop games for work, not to make art. Some games are artistic, others are products. It is the same in cinema, photography, etc. This is something people just do not seem to understand.

replies.author: Daniele-Fantastico
replies.body: There is a whole niche of Desktop Idle or pet-style games that is very successful, like Bongo Cat. These are games that keep you company while you are doing something else. In our case, we added a lot of strategy to the upgrade phase. Considering the target audience, to simplify things we also introduced a feature that automatically applies upgrades. Some people just want a game that progresses on its own, without having to do anything. The "drill" includes a considerable number of funny messages that break up the routine of tedious work, along with lots of easter eggs that make you smile. I have personally used this type of game, and they are interesting. If you do not understand them or do not like them, you can simply move on.

replies.author: Daniele-Fantastico
replies.body: At the moment, AI is not a magic wand. When it comes to writing code, at least for certain languages, it has reached incredible levels. For creativity, it still has issues. In my case, I went through a month of iterations, making changes and testing, to arrive at the current gameplay. It may seem simple, but it is not at all. Balancing, breaking the sense of boredom, avoiding being overly intrusive... all things I had to evaluate personally through long testing sessions. Of course, we are not talking about an artistic or AA game, it is a product that fits into a niche that is currently very popular. I would love to make only artistic games, but from direct experience, they usually sell very little.

replies.author: Daniele-Fantastico
replies.body: Between one major game and the next, it is relaxing to work on something simpler and with more freedom. If I had done everything by hand, it would have taken more time, but I would have ended up with exactly the same result. I know the video game market well. As it is, it suits the niche it was designed for. Obviously, it is not a work of art, and it is not a big game, it was never meant to be. I only asked how others respond to AI-hater comments. Just those. As for the rest of the comments and feedback, having published around twenty games, it is not an issue. I do not have anything left to prove.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body: In your opinion, how should solo indie devs navigate this landscape? I am still struggling to even get some small success? Got any tips?

replies.author: Daniele-Fantastico
replies.body:
Unfortunately, for solo developers it has always been very difficult. We are a small team, and it is still extremely hard. In this sense, AI has not really changed anything, at least not yet. You have to create something very original and innovative, but that is not enough. You also need to do marketing, have a detailed plan months in advance, many months before release. You also have to be a bit of an entrepreneur.  
We have published a lot of games, and sometimes the commercial success has come from the ones we considered less goo or lower quality. The market can be strange at times.

Everyone talks about art, but if you want to sell, then you are making a product. Unfortunately, regardless of a game's quality, only a very small percentage manages to generate a financial return.

Try following the advice of Chris Zukowski. It will not work miracles, but it can significantly increase your chances of success.

replies.author: Daniele-Fantastico
replies.body: The fact that you can’t move horizontally is intentional. It’s not a mobile game. It’s a desktop idle game, and it should be evaluated in that context. The gameplay is about not having to do anything, the game is meant to keep you company. There are many games that work this way. I added a skill tree and a prestige system, but since many players of this genre don’t feel like engaging with upgrades, I introduced a mode that applies them automatically. That’s how it works, and it works well. It might not appeal to everyone, but it’s a niche, and a fairly large one considering how successful some of these games are. I removed comments that were purely from AI haters, as they weren’t useful in any way. Other comments, including those about the gameplay, are not a problem, even when they come from people who aren’t the target audience.

It was something I personally found fun and innovative.

replies.author: Daniele-Fantastico
replies.body: I didn’t ask for feedback on the game. The game is fine as it is. It’s good enough, and the gameplay works very well. When developing a game, there are budgets, target audiences, pricing, and many other factors. If the response from the target players is positive, only then will we spend more time on it and improve it based on their feedback. It’s clearly a low-budget product that will have a very low sale price. It’s our first Desktop Idle Game, and jumping straight into developing a more demanding game without testing the market wouldn’t make sense. It’s one of the things I learned the hard way after publishing more than 20 games on PC and consoles, some low-budget, others definitely not.
